strengths: Addresses a practical problem: improving video generation through inexpensive, training-free selection of initial noise using internal model signals.
Reports improvements on both CogVideoX-2B and 5B, with 4,730 generated videos per configuration and measured inference overheads of approximately 9% and 14%.

Includes useful ablations on acquisition functions, candidate-pool size, stochastic sample count, reversed selection, layer truncation, and scoring timesteps. Truncated scoring reportedly preserves most of the full-layer performance.
weaknesses: The central objective is inconsistent with the implemented algorithm. Equations (4) and (8) define negative Jensen–Shannon disagreement, so minimizing them maximizes disagreement. Appendix B implements the opposite sign while incorrectly asserting that minimization preserves rankings. The implementation may be sensible, but it selects the opposite seeds from the main mathematical specification.

The Bayesian and confidence interpretations are insufficiently justified. Randomly masking fixed attention logits does not establish posterior parameter uncertainty or approximate a specified Bayesian predictive distribution. Moreover, identical uniform attention maps yield zero disagreement, so Proposition 1 does not establish confident or sharp attention. The proposition is a standard consequence of strict entropy concavity, providing limited theoretical novelty.

Comparative evaluation is inadequate. FreeInit and FreqPrior are omitted, yet the paper claims comparable or superior quality and substantial relative efficiency. Those claims require direct evidence. Comparisons against other inexpensive seed-ranking heuristics and compute-matched additional denoising would help establish the method's practical advantage.

Reported improvements are modest and lack confidence intervals, repeated-run variability, or paired significance analysis. Both tested models belong to the same CogVideoX family, which does not support claims of generalization across diverse architectures. Qualitative examples provide limited evidence of perceptual benefit without a human evaluation.

The layer-selection procedure is contradictory. Section 3.3 correlates cumulative scores with full-layer scores across seeds, whereas Appendix E averages across seeds and correlates cumulative scores with video quality. These procedures establish different properties; averaging away seed variation cannot validate within-prompt seed ranking. Calibration prompts also come from VBench, without a clearly documented held-out evaluation split.

Reproducibility and reporting need improvement. Attention type, head aggregation, dropout implementation, and memory-efficient score computation are insufficiently specified, and unchanged memory usage is asserted without measurements. Table 1's CogVideoX-5B total of 81.71 and stated gain of 0.25 are inconsistent with its baseline of 81.52; the appendix's stated weighting instead gives 81.78 from the reported component scores.

Includes useful controls comparing entropy, dropout, Bernoulli masking, reversed selection, and full versus truncated layer evaluation. Qualitative examples illustrate potential benefits, and failure cases are acknowledged.

Appendix B switches the sign while retaining minimization and incorrectly claims that ordering and selection remain unchanged. The implementation may be sensible, but it does not implement the main-text objective.

The Bayesian and confidence interpretations are insufficiently justified. Bernoulli perturbations of fixed attention logits are not established posterior samples, as the paper itself acknowledges. Moreover, identical uniform attention maps yield zero disagreement despite maximal entropy, so Proposition 1 does not establish confident or sharp attention. The proposition is a standard consequence of strict entropy concavity, providing limited theoretical novelty.

Layer selection is described inconsistently. Section 3.3 correlates cumulative scores with full-layer scores across seeds, whereas Appendix E averages over seeds and correlates cumulative scores with official quality scores. These are materially different procedures; the latter also cannot establish within-prompt seed-ranking reliability. Calibration/evaluation separation is unclear because calibration prompts come from VBench.

Evaluation does not establish competitiveness against existing methods or alternative uses of the additional compute. FreeInit and FreqPrior are omitted, yet Section 4 claims comparable or superior quality to them. There is no matched-runtime baseline using additional denoising steps or another competitive selection method. Testing two sizes of one model family also does not support broad architectural generalization.

The improvements are modest and lack uncertainty estimates or repeated independent candidate pools. Table 1 reports a 5B total-score gain of +0.25, although its displayed totals imply +0.19 and its component scores imply approximately +0.26. This inconsistency is material relative to the claimed improvement. Human preference evidence and quantitative within-prompt score–quality correlations are also absent.

Important implementation and efficiency details remain unresolved, including attention-head aggregation, token subsets, dropout configuration, mask handling, and peak memory. Multiplying logits by zero does not remove attention entries after softmax. The claim of unchanged memory requires evidence given the additional stochastic attention calculations.

Several ablation interpretations exceed their evidence. At K=1, the disagreement score is identically zero for every seed, so Table 3 should explain tie-breaking and its relationship to random selection. Saturation at K=10 is not demonstrated by testing only values up to 10. These issues, together with the score and calibration contradictions, substantially weaken reproducibility.

Appendix B implements the opposite sign but incorrectly claims that negation preserves rankings and minimization behavior. This changes which seed the algorithm selects and requires correction throughout the method.

strengths: The problem is practically relevant: selecting initial noise using early model signals could improve video generation without retraining or completing multiple candidate videos.

The reported results are promising. Table 4 shows total VBench improvements of 1.35, 0.63, and 0.19 points on AnimateDiff, CogVideoX-2B, and CogVideoX-5B, respectively, with approximately 9–13% additional runtime. Combining ANSE with FreqPrior provides further gains.

The evaluation covers several backbones and includes useful controls: entropy and dropout alternatives, reversed selection, candidate-pool size, masking probability, layer truncation, additional denoising steps, FVMD, and human preferences.
weaknesses: The central uncertainty interpretation is not established. BANSA is a Jensen–Shannon divergence between attention maps, and Proposition 1 establishes agreement, not confidence: identical uniform maps also yield zero. Masking a fixed attention map does not by itself constitute posterior sampling or establish epistemic uncertainty. The paper acknowledges the absence of a full Bayesian derivation, but still repeatedly makes stronger claims than its mathematics supports.

The masking definition contradicts the ablation description. Under Section 3.2, masks follow Bernoulli(p) and multiply attention entries, so p=0 produces entirely zero rows with undefined renormalization, while p=1 produces identical maps and zero BANSA. Section 6 instead describes p=0 as disabling masking and p=1 as fully random masking. Table 10 therefore cannot be reproduced from the stated algorithm without additional conventions.

There are substantial unresolved reporting inconsistencies. Tables 5 and 19 give exactly identical HunyuanVideo and Wan2.1 values for five quality dimensions, for both baseline and ANSE, despite different backbones. Wan2.1 values also differ substantially from those in the later ablations without a clear explanation of the experimental distinction. These issues require corrected tables or supporting results before the claimed cross-model robustness can be trusted.

The layer-selection procedure is inconsistent across sections. Section 3.3 and Figure 7 correlate partial scores with full-layer BANSA, whereas Appendix D describes correlation with official quality scores after averaging over seeds. These are different procedures, and the latter's positive threshold also conflicts with the claimed negative score–quality relationship. The paper does not establish a disjoint calibration set or demonstrate that correlations across prompt averages preserve within-prompt seed rankings.

The statistical evidence does not adequately establish the reliability of the smaller improvements. Appendix J constructs confidence intervals from ten random subsets of existing videos, rather than documenting independent generation repetitions or a paired analysis accounting for prompts. Several metrics decrease, and many reported intervals overlap. Pooled score–quality correlations also do not establish the within-prompt ranking accuracy needed for seed selection.

The human-study protocol contains a consequential ambiguity: Appendix K says paired baseline and ANSE videos use identical noise seeds, although changing the selected seed is the method's only intervention. It needs to distinguish shared candidate pools from shared selected seeds and explain how judgments and uncertainty were aggregated.

The contribution is primarily an empirical adaptation of BALD/Jensen–Shannon disagreement to attention; the theoretical result is a standard entropy-concavity property. Although the included ablations are useful, comparisons with alternative inexpensive attention-stability scores or other candidate-ranking methods remain limited. Reproducibility is further weakened by missing details on attention-head aggregation, zero-row handling, and implementation of attention scoring; the claim of unchanged memory usage is not supported by memory measurements.

strengths: The paper addresses a practical problem: selecting better initial noise for video diffusion without retraining. Evaluating candidates at the first denoising step and truncating attention-layer computation offers a potentially useful quality–cost tradeoff.

The reported evaluation spans multiple architectures and model sizes. Table 4 reports VBench total-score improvements of 1.35 points for AnimateDiff, 0.63 for CogVideoX-2B, and 0.19 for CogVideoX-5B, with approximately 9–16% inference overhead across the main backbones.

The experiments include useful controls: entropy and dropout alternatives, reversed selection, candidate-pool and masking ablations, full versus truncated scoring, additional sampling steps, and compatibility with FreqPrior. FVMD results and a blinded human preference study provide evidence beyond the main VBench aggregates.
weaknesses: The central Bayesian interpretation is insufficiently justified. Independently masking a fixed attention map measures sensitivity to an imposed perturbation; it does not establish posterior parameter uncertainty or approximate stochastic model predictions without additional assumptions. The footnote acknowledging the absence of a posterior derivation does not establish the claimed epistemic interpretation. Proposition 1 is a standard Jensen–Shannon divergence property and proves agreement, not confidence: identical uniform attention maps also yield zero BANSA.

The masking specification conflicts with its ablation. Section 3.2 defines masks drawn from Bernoulli(p) and multiplies attention by them, so p=0 produces all-zero rows that cannot be normalized, while p=1 leaves every map unchanged and yields zero disagreement. Section 6 instead describes p=0 as disabling masking and p=1 as fully random masking. The implementation, zero-row handling, and interpretation of Table 10 therefore require clarification.

There are substantial unresolved numerical inconsistencies. In Table 5, HunyuanVideo and Wan2.1 have exactly identical baseline and selected scores across five quality dimensions; these duplicated means recur in Table 19. Meanwhile, the Wan2.1 values in Tables 10, 15, and 16 differ substantially from Table 5 without a clear reconciliation of settings. These issues weaken confidence in the claimed cross-backbone replication and require corrected tables and traceable evaluation outputs.

The layer-selection procedure is contradictory. Section 3.3 and Figure 7 select depth using correlation with the full-layer BANSA score, whereas Appendix D describes correlation with official quality scores after averaging over seeds. The latter introduces quality supervision and does not test whether truncated scores preserve within-prompt seed rankings. Its positive correlation threshold also conflicts with the claimed negative score–quality relationship. The paper needs one reproducible procedure and an explicit separation between calibration and evaluation prompts.

The statistical and human-study protocols do not adequately resolve the small gains. Appendix J constructs confidence intervals from ten random subsets of 100 existing videos, without clearly specifying the estimator or accounting for prompt clustering and paired comparisons; these are not independent generation replications. Several metrics decrease, and uncertainty on aggregate improvements is absent. Appendix K also states that baseline and ANSE videos use identical noise seeds, which is inconsistent with a method whose sole intervention is seed selection unless this means a shared candidate pool. The actual pairing protocol needs clarification.

The novelty and empirical advantage of the particular acquisition function remain only partially established. BANSA transfers an existing disagreement functional to attention, and the practical method uses synthetic masking of a deterministic map. The entropy comparison is useful, but attention-concentration statistics and other inexpensive seed-ranking alternatives would better establish whether masking adds meaningful information. Pooled score–quality correlations across prompts do not establish the within-prompt ranking accuracy needed by the method.

Several broader claims exceed the evidence. Spatial intra-frame variance does not demonstrate dynamic expressiveness, and the cross-prompt analysis uses only one transferred seed and two destination prompts. Semantic evaluation is omitted for HunyuanVideo and Wan2.1, while some quality metrics regress. Given these limitations and the unresolved methodological and reporting inconsistencies, the promising empirical direction is not yet supported strongly enough for acceptance.

strengths: The paper addresses a practically relevant problem: selecting better initial noise for video diffusion without retraining. Scoring candidates at the first denoising step using truncated network execution is an appealing approach.

The reported experiments span several architectures and model sizes. Table 4 reports VBench total-score improvements of 1.35 points on AnimateDiff, 0.63 on CogVideoX-2B, and 0.19 on CogVideoX-5B, with approximately 9–13% runtime overhead.

The evaluation includes useful ablations on entropy versus disagreement, masking versus dropout, candidate-pool size, layer truncation, and reversed selection. Compatibility with FreqPrior, additional FVMD results, and a human preference study broaden the empirical evidence.
weaknesses: The central uncertainty interpretation is insufficiently justified. BANSA is a Jensen–Shannon divergence between perturbed attention distributions, but masking a fixed attention map is not demonstrated to approximate posterior model samples or epistemic uncertainty. Proposition 1 establishes agreement, not confidence: identical uniform attention maps also yield zero BANSA. Consequently, the repeated claim that minimization ensures both confident and consistent attention does not follow from the theory.

There are substantial numerical reporting inconsistencies. In Table 5, HunyuanVideo and Wan2.1 have exactly identical baseline and proposed-method values across five quality dimensions; these entries recur in Table 19. These require verification before accepting the cross-model evidence. Also, AnimateDiff with ANSE has quality 81.66 and semantic 71.09, which yield approximately 79.55 under the stated 4:1 aggregation, rather than the reported total of 79.33.

The layer-selection procedure is contradictory. Section 3.3 and Figure 7 correlate partial-layer scores with full-layer scores, whereas Appendix D describes correlation with official quality scores after averaging over seeds. These are different procedures, and a positive quality correlation also conflicts with the claimed negative BANSA–quality relationship. The calibration/evaluation split is unspecified, and correlation across prompt averages does not establish preservation of within-prompt seed rankings.

The masking ablation is inconsistent with the mathematical definition. Under Bernoulli(p) multiplicative masking, p=0 produces all-zero rows that cannot be normalized, while p=1 produces identical maps and zero disagreement. Section 6 instead describes these settings as disabling masking and fully random masking, respectively. The implementation convention, handling of empty rows, and tie-breaking need clarification.

Statistical and human-evaluation protocols leave important uncertainty. Appendix J constructs confidence intervals from repeated subsets of generated videos, without clearly accounting for prompt clustering or reporting paired differences. This does not establish independent-run robustness. Appendix K states that baseline and ANSE videos use identical noise seeds, which is incompatible with attributing differences solely to seed selection under otherwise identical deterministic sampling; the intended pairing must be explained.

The empirical advantage is promising but not yet sufficiently established for acceptance. Several gains are small or mixed, semantic evaluation is omitted for HunyuanVideo and Wan2.1, and acquisition-function comparisons are limited to one backbone. Stronger compute-matched seed-selection baselines and within-prompt ranking analyses would help establish the value of the proposed statistic. The unresolved methodological and reporting issues outweigh the breadth of the reported experiments.
